tier_reason: First-party arXiv preprint (2505.11480, not peer-reviewed as far as seen) whose headline numbers (95.0% pass, 1.46x over gcc -O3; Claude-opus-4 51.5%, 1.43x; base Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 61.4%, 1.10x) were confirmed only through WebSearch snippets because arxiv.org and alphaxiv.org are blocked; the public harness (src/test_benchmark.py, hyperfine) exists but no CPU model or gcc version is stated in the repo, and the released dataset scripts do not match the paper's -O3 baseline, so not A or B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Per the paper (snippet only): baseline assembly from gcc -O3. Released scripts: src/create_data/convert_to_hf_raw.py emits gcc -O0 -S (stored as 'unoptimized_assembly', the prompt input and the timing baseline) and gcc -O3 -S (stored as the reference answer); all assembly is linked with plain 'gcc file.s -o bin -lm'; gcc version not stated. Timing: hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10, mean whole-process wall time per test input, up to 10 inputs per program.
corrections.caveats: Headline numbers come from WebSearch snippets of arXiv 2505.11480 (paper not opened; arXiv and alphaXiv blocked); the README has no results section and states no hardware or gcc version. The released harness (src/test_benchmark.py) floors every per-input speedup at 1.0 ('If generated code is slower, set speedup to 1.0'), gives failed, non-compiling or benchmark-failing cases a speedup of 1.0 (they are averaged in as 1.0, not excluded), and treats output identical to the baseline assembly as correct at 1.0 without running it, so the reported average can never fall below 1.0 and is biased upward. In the released dataset-building scripts (src/create_data/convert_to_hf_raw.py, create_top_speedup.py) the 'unoptimized_assembly' that test_benchmark.py times against is gcc -O0 output, while the paper says the baseline is gcc -O3; the published HuggingFace dataset (LLM4Code/llm_superoptimizer_ds) could not be opened to check which variant the reported numbers used, so the repo as released does not demonstrably reproduce the -O3 comparison. Correctness is checked on at most 10 CodeNet test inputs per program, and timings are whole-process (startup included) on small competitive-programming programs, run concurrently in a thread pool. The output is a fine-tuned model (HuggingFace LLM4Code/Superoptimizer_Qwen7B, licence not checked), not a library; the repo is a 2-commit code drop. Preprint status.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2 stars, 0 forks; model weights published as LLM4Code/Superoptimizer_Qwen7B on HuggingFace

notes: Repo, Apache-2.0 licence, 2 stars and last commit 2025-10-23 (2 commits, both that day) confirmed on github.com; still 'active' until 2026-10-23. Shortcomings to record: speedup floored at 1.0 per input and failures averaged in as 1.0 (record's caveat said failures were excluded; corrected), released scripts time against gcc -O0 assembly while the paper claims gcc -O3 (unresolved, HF dataset unreachable), no CPU or gcc version, preprint numbers seen only in search snippets. Not invalid evidence, so kept at C.

tier_reason: The only numbers are a single forum user's (jj2007, masm32.com, April 2020) assemble times of a 21,000-line source, confirmed by a second WebSearch snippet but not openable here (masm32.com ENOTFOUND); an anecdote without hardware, versions or method is C at most, kept at C under the harness's snippet-only rule.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (masm32.com forum post by jj2007, April 2020, not opened): on a 21,000-line source, MASM 6.15 1800 ms, MASM 10.0 1800 ms, UAsm64 1630 ms, JWasm 1480 ms, AsmC 1200 ms (UASM about 1.1x faster than MASM, derived from snippet data). Same thread, m32lib samples: UAsm64 7285 ClockTicks vs JWasm 4867 and AsmC 4181 (no MASM figure in the snippet). The README makes no speed claim.
corrections.caveats: Numbers seen only in WebSearch snippets of masm32.com forum posts (site unreachable here: ENOTFOUND); single user, one machine, no hardware, flags or exact versions. The margin over MASM is small (about 1.1x) and UASM is the slowest of the three MASM-compatible open assemblers in the same test: JWasm (1480 ms) and AsmC (1200 ms) are faster, and on the m32lib samples UAsm64 took about 1.5x JWasm's and 1.7x AsmC's ClockTicks; another forum member calls UASM 'rather slow' compared with other assemblers. UASM descends from JWasm via HJWasm (the README's chat link is still named HJWASM) but is not a GitHub fork. Last commit 2022-03-16 on the only branch (master), no releases on GitHub; project site terraspace.co.uk unreachable here. Licence is the Sybase Open Watcom Public License 1.0 (OSI-approved; GitHub's sidebar does not name it).

notes: Repo confirmed: 271 stars, 62 forks, 673 commits, not archived, last commit 2022-03-16 (abandoned, over 3 years), Watcom-1.0 licence text in README. Shortcomings: anecdotal snippet-only forum timing, only about 1.1x over MASM 6.15/10.0, slower than JWasm and AsmC (both already in wave 13 merged.json as baron-von-riedesel/jwasm and nidud/asmc), abandoned. A masm32 forum snippet also says AsmC is 25-30% faster than UAsm and 7-8x faster than MASM (MASM version unstated), which hints that newer ML versions may be much slower than the 6.15/10.0 figures; not usable as a number without the page.

tier_reason: No SLOTHY-attributable measured speedup was reachable: the peer-reviewed TCHES 2024 paper (issue 1, pp. 87-132; eprint 2022/1303) is blocked and its abstract snippet only says the optimized code matches or beats prior art; the repo's README is directional, its tutorial gives only an LLVM-MCA model estimate for a toy loop, and the paper artifact (paper/, pqax, pqmx) needs boards that were not run.

corrections.caveats: The TCHES 2024 paper 'Fast and Clean: Auditable high-performance assembly via constraint solving' (issue 1, pp. 87-132, artifact at artifacts.iacr.org/tches/2024/a6; eprint 2022/1303) is peer-reviewed but could not be opened (tches.iacr.org and eprint unreachable); WebSearch snippets only say the SLOTHY-optimized code matches or beats prior art in all cases, with no cycle counts. The repo ships clean and optimized sources (paper/clean, paper/opt), optimization scripts (paper/scripts) and a Docker artifact; cycle benchmarks live in pqax/pqmx and need Cortex-A55/A72 devices or an MPS3 FPGA board (AN547/AN555), and builds without CYCLES=PMU/PERF stub out cycle counts. The only number in the repo is the tutorial's LLVM-MCA model estimate for a toy Cortex-A55 loop (31 to 21 cycles per iteration), a model output against its own unscheduled input, not a measurement. Adoption is real: s2n-bignum PR #108 (merged 2024-02-15) imported the SLOTHY-generated Lenngren-based X25519 without benchmark numbers; the AWS-LC PR #1469 that reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup', Graviton 2) was closed without merge on 2024-03-06 (the README calls it merged) and mixes the algorithm change with SLOTHY scheduling. CP-SAT is non-deterministic, so re-optimization results vary, especially for the heuristic Cortex-A72 model. SLOTHY is a Python tool that produces assembly; it is not linked into the user's program.

notes: Repo confirmed: MIT (LICENSE file, SPDX MIT), 352 stars, 45 forks, not archived, last commit 2026-10-02 (active), PyPI package 'slothy'. Notable despite under 1k stars (TCHES paper, used by s2n-bignum/AWS-LC, CMSIS-DSP via Arm EndpointAI, mlkem-native), so kept at D rather than rejected. Paper-access retier candidate: with the TCHES 2024 tables plus the public pqax/pqmx harness and named cores it could reach B (or A if pqax/pqmx Makefiles give compiler and flags).
